records.name: Edo
records.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

sources.summary: Nigerian Observer (May 2018): in Ekpoma a mob lynched one of two men caught together and the other escaped, framed as an 'abominable act' under traditional heritage. Documents fatal community violence in Edo State.

The Initiative for Equal Rights (TIERs) '2024 Human Rights Violations Report' (published January 2025): annual documentation of violations based on real or perceived SOGIESC in Nigeria; per the dossier, its 2024 edition records 556 violations affecting 850 victims across the reporting period and states these represent only a fraction of the true scale.

On 10 June 2010 The Nigerian Observer reported from Benin City (Oredo LGA, Edo State) that a middle-aged man, Mark Osato Edomwonyi, narrowly escaped being killed by a mob after he was caught in a same-sex act with his partner Paddy in Paddy's rented apartment; a neighbour raised the alarm and Mark fled through the backyard before the mob arrived, which then 'unleashed terror' on Paddy. No police intervention, arrest or prosecution is recorded in the report, and Mark's whereabouts were still unknown at filing. First incident-level evidence for Edo beyond the 2018 Ekpoma killing: lethal mob 'community justice' operates in the state capital too, with no documented law-enforcement response.

The Nigerian Observer reported on 15 August 2008 that police declared Ugbogbo Ovbukhan wanted over 'gay practice' after he and his partner Jerry were caught in the act in a remote community in Edo State in February 2008; a mob mercilessly beat the two for desecrating the community, Ovbukhan escaped before police arrived, and the police arrested Jerry for interrogation. Direct evidence that Edo's police machinery pursued same-sex couples on the ground in 2008 — a community lynching attempt answered by arrest and a wanted declaration rather than protection.

records.name: Aceh
records.summary:
Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own — the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) — which criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. The penalty scale runs up to 100 strokes for morality offences, and courts apply it publicly: in August 2025 a Sharia court sitting behind closed doors sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual

sources.summary: QURU: Journal of Family Law and Culture (doi 10.59698/quru.v3i1.405): 'The Increasing Number of Waria in Banda Aceh: Between Social Challenges and Law Enforcement' by UIN Ar-Raniry scholars (keywords: Law Enforcement, Waria, Aceh, Islamic Law, Qanun). Aceh legal scholarship analysing the rise of waria cases through a sharia-law-enforcement lens — the academic counterpart to the record's enforcement claims.

CBS News/AP (26 Aug 2025): two men were publicly caned in conservative Aceh province after a sharia court convicted them of hugging and kissing — the documented Aug-2025 caning episode the record's summary is built on, confirming public caning as the province's signature punishment.

iNews Aceh (undated local report, Feb-2025 round-up context): Satpol PP and Wilayatul Hisbah Banda Aceh secured an alleged gay couple in a boarding house; a local advocate urged police to investigate and boarding-house owners to monitor tenants. Supports the record's Feb-2025 enforcement-reaches-trans-people claim.

UNSW Human Rights Research Centre: transgender women face the highest rates of violence among LGBTIQ Indonesians, with survey data on relative social hostility; underpins this record's Indonesia-wide trans-violence context including the Jan-2018 twelve-transwomen detention claim that no Aceh-specific source in this record covers (rule-5 keep).

records.name: Lampung
records.summary:
In November 2018 Satpol PP, the regional moral-and-order force, raided three transwomen in Lampung — an incident a comparative UNSW/Harvard review of violence against transgender women in this country records as police-perpetrated violence. No further incidents, arrests, or enacted local bylaws specific to Lampung were found in the dossier period, and no visitor-facing documents or screening information is recorded.

For a visitor, the practical exposure is a single documented police-contact incident with no campaign evidence: the raid shows that police contact can escalate into documented police-perpetrated violence, but the dossier does not support a patterned risk.

sources.summary: UNSW human-rights review of anti-trans violence in Indonesia: documents that in November 2018 three transwomen were raided by Satpol PP (the regional morals-and-order force) in Lampung province — detained at the Satpol PP office and hosed down at the firefighter building, with an officer recording it — alongside a national pattern of transwomen murdered in 2017 (Bone, Semarang, South Sulawesi) and election-cycle anti-LGBT bylaw lobbying from 2016 onward; an SMRC survey of 1,520 Indonesians (Nov 2016) found LGBT people hated by 16.6%.

OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation study analyses discriminatory regional regulations in eight Indonesian provinces — Aceh, DKI Jakarta, East Kalimantan, Lampung, North Sumatera, South Sulawesi, South Sumatera and Yogyakarta — at province and district level; Lampung is named among them, supporting this record's claim of discriminatory regional regulation. records.name: Central Kalimantan
records.summary:
Central Kalimantan shows no sub-national divergence for a visitor: no enacted discriminatory bylaw, raid, arrest or incident series targeting transgender people was found, and the province is not one of the eight identified in OutRight International's Creeping Criminalisation analysis of discriminatory regional regulations. Visitor risk therefore tracks the national baseline: the KUHP criminal code in force from 1 January 2026 criminalises sexual activity outside marriage, with unmarried partners facing up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member; because same-sex marriage is not recognised, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction.

Ordinary local moral policing seen in some neighbouring provinces is absent here, but there is no province-specific enforcement record in either direction; any risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence, and a transgender visitor should assume the national criminal baseline applies in full.

sources.summary: OutRight Action International, 'Creeping Criminalisation' (Katjasungkana & Wieringa, 2022): mapping of national laws and regional regulations violating rights of women and LGBTIQ people in Indonesia; its eight-province list of discriminatory regional regulations does NOT include Central Kalimantan, which is the basis for treating the earlier 'one of the eight provinces' attribution for this unit as a misplacement of East Kalimantan.

Wikipedia's article on the 2023 Indonesian Penal Code (RUU KUHP) records that the law was passed on 6 December 2022 and took effect on 2 January 2026, three years after enactment, and that it criminalises sexual activity outside marriage — unmarried partners face up to one year in prison if a complaint is lodged by an immediate family member. The article notes the code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex relationships, and that because same-sex marriage is not recognised in Indonesia, all sexual activity by same-sex couples falls under that outside-marriage restriction. This is the national criminal baseline a visitor in Central Kalimantan stands under, consistent with this record's finding that the province's risk follows the country's national framework rather than a local divergence.
